ch00.note: So popular was The Whistling Wind on its serialization in 1943 that publishers dubbed the year 徐觑年, ‘the Year of Xu Xu’—a description borne out by scholarship on the period. This ‘About the Author’ page is the source edition’s own front matter, not written by Xu Xu.

ch00.anchor: Yu Lihua, Ji Zheng and Nie Hualing
ch00.note: Three writers of the postwar Chinese diaspora. Yu Lihua (於梨華, 1929–2020) and Nie Hualing (聚華艮, 1925–2024, co-founder of the Iowa International Writing Program) are well documented; Ji Zheng (吉鈕) was a Taiwanese novelist of the same ‘overseas-student’ school, more thinly recorded.

ch01.note: C. L. Stephen, an American naval medical officer and soon the narrator’s closest friend, whose acquaintance the following chapters recount. The name 史蒂芬 transliterates the English ‘Stephen.’

ch02.anchor: the foreign concessions still kept their peculiar standing
ch02.note: After Japan occupied the Chinese-administered districts of Shanghai in 1937, the foreign concessions—the International Settlement and the French Concession—stayed under British, American, French and other control, policed by their own garrisons, until Japan seized them after Pearl Harbor in December 1941. This anomalous enclave was known as the Solitary Island (see Chapter 3).

ch03.note: 孤岛 (gudao), the name for the foreign concessions of Shanghai in 1937–41, when they survived as islands of neutral territory ringed by Japanese-held China. Also Englished as the ‘isolated’ or ‘orphan’ island.
Bai Ping (白芨), a dancer at the Paramount and one of the three women at the novel’s centre; she is introduced in the next chapter.

ch04.note: William Hazlitt’s Table-Talk (two volumes, 1821–22) is a real collection of familiar essays; the piece the narrator recalls is most likely ‘On Living to One’s-Self,’ Hazlitt’s meditation on a life led apart from the world.

ch04.anchor: A camellia that belongs to any man
ch04.note: The exchange sets a rose (which belongs to no one) against a camellia (which belongs to any man). In its literary code the camellia is the flower of the courtesan—as in Dumas’s La Dame aux camélias (茶花女)—and Bai Ping applies it to herself, a dance-hostess.
St Ignatius Cathedral at Xujiahui (older spelling Zikawei), in southwest Shanghai: a Gothic church built by French Jesuits in 1906–10 and the seat of Shanghai Catholicism.

ch05.anchor: a heart as solemn and translucent as this
ch05.note: The source text of this clause is garbled—愿我用就有这样庄严与透明的心灵, in which 用就 appears to be a corruption of 永/永远 (‘always’). The sense ‘may I too always have a heart as solemn and translucent as this’ is rendered here; the defect is left visible rather than silently smoothed over.

ch06.note: A pun: 红心 is at once the winning red of the roulette table where they had gambled, the ‘hearts’ of a card suit, and a ‘red heart’ in the sense of sincerity—so that her stake was laid on his affections.

ch07.note: In Greek myth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection and pined away into the flower that bears his name. The source uses an older, now-superseded transliteration, 纳虚仙子 (modern 纳西索斯).
Claude Debussy (1862–1918), French composer, a central figure of musical Impressionism.
Helen, a shy, music-loving young American, the third of the novel’s principal women. Her surname, 曼斯儿, transliterates a Western name the source does not spell out; ‘Manfield’ is a reconstruction.

ch08.note: The orchestra of the Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局), long conducted by Mario Paci and reckoned the finest in the Far East; it gave the Chinese premiere of Beethoven’s Ninth in 1936, and a 1939 performance paired it with a large local chorus. The narrator’s explanation that the concert was moved to the evening because the chorus could not all be free by day is his own detail, not independently corroborated.
Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), German Idealist philosopher, a contemporary of Fichte and Hegel—fitting reading for a narrator at work on a book about ethics and aesthetics.

ch09.note: The narrator’s reading runs Western and Chinese together: after the German Idealist Schelling comes a name the source prints as ‘Eicht,’ almost certainly a garbling of Fichte (Johann Gottlieb Fichte, 1762–1814), Schelling’s fellow Idealist; then Bergson, and the Daoist sage Zhuangzi and the Song poet Su Dongpo (Su Shi). The defective spelling is rendered to sense and left visible.

ch09.anchor: Major General Suzuki Jiro and Colonel Yamao Motohara
ch09.note: Bai Ping mischievously supplies the two Japanese officers’ ranks—shao jiang (少将, major general) and da zuo (大佐, the Imperial Japanese Army rank of colonel)—where Mei Yingzi had given only names, marking them at once as senior figures and sounding the espionage note beneath the party’s surface. The names 铅木次郎 and 山尾本原 are read here in their Japanese forms.

Mario Paci (梅百器, Mei Baiqi, 1878–1946), the Italian pianist and conductor who led the Shanghai Municipal Orchestra from 1919 to 1942 (see Chapter 8) and trained many of China’s first Western-schooled musicians; that Helen studies under him marks her as seriously trained. Corroborated by the historical record.

ch10.note: Reverie is Träumerei (‘Dreaming’), the seventh and most famous piece of Robert Schumann’s Kinderszenen (Scenes from Childhood, Op. 15, 1838).

ch10.anchor: the little garret over the stair-landing
ch10.note: The tingzijian (亭子间), the small, cheaply let room over the stair-landing at the back of a Shanghai lane-house—between floors, north-facing, cramped and cold, and in this period a byword for the lodgings of writers and students.

ch12.note: North Sichuan Road (北四川路) ran through Hongkou, the district north of Suzhou Creek that was the centre of Shanghai’s Japanese population and, from 1937, effectively under Japanese control, its crossings from the concessions guarded by Japanese sentries. Hence the narrator, coming from the concessions, had not set foot there since the fall of the Chinese-administered city, and the way to the station runs past enemy sentries and hoardings for chouhuo (仇货, ‘enemy goods’)—the Japanese-made goods patriotic Shanghai had boycotted. Corroborated.

Geling (葛崍, Ge Ridge), a hill on the north shore of the West Lake at Hangzhou, named for the Jin-dynasty alchemist and Daoist Ge Hong, who is said to have refined his elixirs there; its Baopu Daoist temple still stands.

ch13.note: The great sights of the West Lake at Hangzhou: the Su Causeway (苏堂), raised by the poet-governor Su Shi (Su Dongpo), and the Bai Causeway (白堂), associated with the poet Bai Juyi; Solitary Hill (孤岛, Gushan), the island hill famous for its plum blossom; and the Three Pools Mirroring the Moon (三潭印月). This is the narrator’s own lost ground, now under enemy occupation.

The National Academy of Art (国立艺术院), founded on the West Lake in 1928 by Cai Yuanpei with Lin Fengmian as its first president; its opening ceremony was held at Solitary Hill. During the war it was evacuated to the interior—which is why the narrator’s friends from it are now ‘scattered.’ Corroborated.

黄锡包 (huang xibao), literally ‘yellow tin-foil pack.’ The premium tinned cigarettes of the British-American Tobacco Company were known in Shanghai by the colour of their packing—white (Capstan), green (Three Castles), red (Ruby Queen)—and the yellow pack was one of these; the exact English brand it names is not certain.

ch14.note: Franz Schubert (1797–1828), the Austrian composer, celebrated above all for his songs (Lieder)—fitting for the piece Helen sings.

Major painters of modern Chinese ink art: Qi Baishi (齐白石, 1864–1957) and Wu Changshuo (吴昌硕, 1844–1927); the landscape on the far wall is by Ren Bonian (任伯年, 1840–1895) of the Shanghai School. Bai Ping’s scrolls mark her taste as cultivated, not merely fashionable.

ch15.note: Wartime Shanghai sheltered a large community of Central European Jewish refugees, who reached the city from 1938 onward because it required no entry visa; many opened cafés and restaurants, and one such stood here on the corner of Route Winling and Avenue Joffre in the French Concession. Corroborated.

The narrator runs through the old definitions of philosophy. ‘The handmaid of religion’ echoes the medieval scholastic tag philosophia ancilla theologiae, ‘philosophy is the handmaid of theology,’ which made philosophy subordinate to religious doctrine; ‘the science of sciences’ is the opposite, later claim for philosophy’s primacy over the special sciences.

Jessfield Park (兆丰公园, Zhaofeng gongyuan), a large public garden in the west of the International Settlement, laid out by the Shanghai Municipal Council in 1914; it was renamed Zhongshan Park in 1941 in memory of Sun Yat-sen, though the novel keeps the older, concession-era name. Corroborated.

ch16.note: Richard Wagner (1813–1883), the German operatic composer; the source gives the name in the Latin alphabet. Reciting a line of Plato and holding forth on Wagner marks the transformed Helen’s new taste for a display of culture.

ch17.note: DD’s Café (弟弟, Didi, ‘little brother’), a fashionable café on Avenue Joffre in the French Concession, a well-known resort of stage and screen people in the Shanghai of these years. Corroborated.

A road in the French Concession (姚主教路, ‘Bishop Yao’s Road’; today Tianping Road), named for the French Jesuit Prosper Paris (Chinese name Yao Zongli), bishop of the Nanjing vicariate, which then included Shanghai. Corroborated.

Tao Yuanming (陶渊明, also Tao Qian, 365–427), the great poet of reclusion and the pastoral, who gave up official life to return to his fields and gardens. His renunciation is the archetype of high-minded withdrawal in the Chinese tradition, so the narrator’s sudden wish to read him marks his own longing to retreat from this glittering, hollow life.

ch18.note: 月宫, the cold and remote lunar palace where the moon-goddess Chang’e dwells alone, having fled there with the stolen elixir of immortality. In the playful exchange the dazzling Mei Yingzi is cast as the sun and the reclusive narrator as one who dreams of light from within the dark earth; the image of a moon-cold seclusion returns through the chapter.

Wu Zetian (武则天, 624–705), the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right, at the height of the Tang; and the Western Empress Dowager—Cixi (慈禧, 1835–1908), who dominated the late Qing court for nearly half a century. Mei Yingzi names them as women who, having missed the radiance of their youth, turned in later life to the grasping of power. Corroborated.
寇莉莎, the drink Mei Yingzi calls for after the narrator’s whisky; the name transliterates an imported drink—a liqueur or cocktail—that the source does not otherwise identify, romanized here as Kolisa.

ch19.note: 宫间登水, the name on the Japanese admirer’s visiting-card. The narrator says outright that he cannot recall it exactly (‘something like’), so the reading is left tentative; the Japanese form given here is one plausible reconstruction, the source supplying no romanization.

An allusion to the Zhuangzi: 君子之交淡若水, ‘the friendship of a gentleman is insipid as water,’ set there against 小人之交甘若醴, ‘the friendship of a mean man is sweet as wine.’ The undemanding, distant friendship keeps its savour, while the cloying, over-close one soon sours; the narrator invokes it to name what he now feels for Mrs. Stephen.

ch20.note: The outbreak of the Pacific war. Because of the date-line the attack on Pearl Harbor of December 7 (Hawaii time) fell on December 8 in Shanghai, and the gunfire the narrator hears in the small hours is the action on the Huangpu: Japanese forces called on the two Allied gunboats lying off the Bund to surrender, sank the British Peterel—whose crew refused and largely died at their posts—and seized the American Wake, whose men were made prisoners. With this the Solitary Island fell and the Japanese entered the foreign concessions. Corroborated.

ch21.note: 浦东, the east bank of the Huangpu opposite the Bund. After Pearl Harbor the Japanese interned Allied nationals in a ring of camps in and around Shanghai—the Woosung and Kiangwan camps for captured service-members, and, from 1943, the Pootung (Pudong) Civil Assembly Centre, in a former warehouse across the river, for enemy civilians. The novel places the captured Stephen ‘on the Pudong side.’ Corroborated in outline.

The Marco Polo Bridge (Lugou Bridge) Incident of July 7, 1937—a clash between Japanese and Chinese troops at the Lugou Bridge southwest of Beijing—which opened the full-scale Sino-Japanese War, China’s War of Resistance. ‘Since July 7’ (七七) became a standard way of dating the war’s beginning. Corroborated.

ch22.note: 赛金花 (c. 1872–1936) was the most celebrated courtesan of the late Qing. Having earlier traveled to Europe in the train of a diplomat and picked up some German, she was said, during the Eight-Nation Alliance's occupation of Beijing after the Boxer Uprising of 1900, to have traded on her acquaintance with the allied commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Alfred von Waldersee, to obtain provisions for the foreign armies and to beg mercy for the people of the city. To call Bai Ping 'a true Sai Jinhua now' is to cast her as a beauty who keeps company with the occupier, at once collaborator and secret protector. Corroborated.

A 钱庄 or native bank, the traditional Chinese banking house of the treaty-port era, which took deposits, made loans, and issued its own drafts and money orders alongside the foreign and modern banks; the Fuyuan is named as the house on which Mei Yingzi's check is drawn.
Source 赛罗凡. A fashionable Shanghai restaurant or nightspot; the name transliterates a Western one that has not been identified with certainty, and is rendered here by its sound.

ch23.note: 石涛 (1642–c. 1707), monk-painter of the early Qing and one of its boldest landscapists, born a scion of the fallen Ming imperial house. A Shitao on the wall marks the taste, and the means, of the study's absent owner. Corroborated.

The digital source prints 任董叔; no calligrapher of that name is known, and it is almost certainly a corruption of 任堇叔, that is 任堇 (Ren Jin, 1881–1936), styled 堇叔, a painter and calligrapher of the late Qing and early Republic. The name is rendered accordingly; the reading is the translator's.

ch25.note: In occupied Shanghai more than one currency circulated at once: the 'national currency' (法币, fabi) of the Nationalist government in Chongqing, and the military notes issued by the Japanese, soon supplemented by the scrip of the collaborationist regime. That Bai Ping's winnings mingle Japanese notes and national currency is a stroke of the city's divided wartime economy.

虹口, the district north of Suzhou Creek that was the heart of Japanese Shanghai, where Japanese residents, troops, and offices were concentrated; here the occupying officers are billeted, the junior men two rooms to a floor and the senior each in a requisitioned house. Corroborated.

ch26.note: The station where Helen sings and reads a little English-language news, 海邻广播电台. After Japan seized the foreign concessions at the end of 1941 it took control of Shanghai broadcasting, and Japanese-controlled stations carried English-language programming as an instrument of occupation propaganda—which is why the narrator, hearing that it is ‘a Japanese station,’ presses Helen on what her work really serves. Corroborated in outline; the fictional station’s name (海邻, Hailin) is not otherwise identified, and is romanized here.

Moving into hiding at Mei Yingzi’s bidding, the narrator takes the assumed name 陈寂 (Chen Ji). The given name 寂 means ‘silence, stillness, solitude’—the very note of quiet withdrawal the solitary philosopher longs for—so that the false name he hides behind still speaks his own truth.

ch29.note: 万国公墓 (Wanguo gongmu, the ‘Cemetery of All Nations’), the Shanghai cemetery for the dead of every nationality, Chinese and foreign alike, opened in the western outskirts early in the twentieth century; here Stephen is buried, and Helen comes at dawn to his grave. Rendered by its customary English name. Corroborated.

The American dancer Isadora Duncan (1877–1927), pioneer of modern dance, who broke from the fixed vocabulary of classical ballet toward free, natural, unfettered movement; the source gives her name, and the word ‘ballet,’ in the Latin alphabet. The figure marks Helen’s return to a natural, unaffected bearing. Corroborated.

ch30.note: The Chinese proverb 真金不怕火炼, ‘true gold fears no refining fire’—the genuine article will stand any test. Helen turns it back on him: if he is true gold, why should he need to keep passing through the fire of these compromising engagements at all?

ch31.note: 大世界 (Da shijie), the celebrated many-storeyed amusement palace at the edge of the French Concession, opened in 1917 and crowded with theatres, restaurants, games, and sideshows—a byword for cheap, teeming popular entertainment, fittingly the setting for the out-of-the-way dance hall Mei Yingzi asks to be taken to. Corroborated.

ch33.note: The grand civic centre at Jiangwan (江湾), north of the old city, raised under the Nationalist government’s ‘Greater Shanghai Plan’ of the early 1930s; its centrepiece, the Shanghai Municipal Government Building, opened in 1933 in a monumental Chinese-palace style. The district fell to the Japanese in 1937 and was turned to military use—which is why an occupying rear admiral is quartered close by. The narrator’s ‘what had once been our’ marks it as a lost emblem of Chinese self-government. Corroborated.

ch33.anchor: the peace of Greater East Asia
ch33.note: Slogans of the occupation and its Chinese collaborators: the ‘peace’ and ‘Sino-Japanese friendship’ (中日联谊) of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere (大东亚共荣圈), the propaganda framework Japan proclaimed in 1940 to dress conquest as liberation. That Bai Ping should mouth them, and crown the enemy’s own agent Mei Yingzi ‘goddess of peace,’ is the bitter irony the narrator hears in words that ‘grated harshly on the ear.’ Corroborated.

ch35.note: The heroine of Ghost Love (鬼恋), Xu Xu’s own 1937 novella, the sensation that made his name: a beautiful, enigmatic woman in black, met by night, who tells the narrator she is a ghost and forbids him to love her. The stone-still, deathly composure the narrator reads in Mei Yingzi’s face borrows that figure—the alluring woman who is more than half a phantom of death. Corroborated.

A literal rendering of the idiom 小鹿乱撞 (xiaolu luan zhuang, ‘a fawn bounding wildly’), the stock Chinese figure for a heart pounding with fright or agitation; the English keeps the image of startled deer leaping in the breast rather than flattening it to ‘my heart raced.’

ch37.anchor: the holy robe of Atri in a novel by Flaubert
ch37.note: The dream-image is offered as a literary allusion, but a garbled one: the source misspells the novelist Gustave Flaubert (1821–1880) as ‘Flaulert,’ and the sacred garment it names—阿特立 (Atri)—cannot be securely matched to any robe in Flaubert’s works, so the name is romanized here as printed and left visible rather than silently ‘corrected.’ What the dream keeps is the image: a shining, magical vestment that draws red ink—blood—and the crowd’s superstitious dread onto whoever dares to wear it, an omen of the gunfire and the bloodstained gown to come.

ch38.note: A port city on the Shandong peninsula, in this period a fashionable seaside summer resort. Leased to Germany as the Kiautschou (Jiaozhou) concession from 1898, seized by Japan in 1914, and restored to Chinese sovereignty in 1922, it was built up with beaches, villas and bathing-grounds that drew wealthy Shanghai holidaymakers and the crews of the foreign warships anchored offshore—the ‘drunken sailors off the Western warships’ of Helen’s letter in the next chapter. Japan reoccupied the city in January 1938; Helen goes there in winter precisely because the summer crowds are gone. Corroborated.

ch39.note: A fictional figure, but a recognizable type. After the Russian Revolution and Civil War of 1917–1922, tens of thousands of White Russian émigrés settled in the cities of China—Harbin, Shanghai, Tianjin, Qingdao—and among them were many trained musicians who lived by giving lessons and filled the ranks of orchestras such as the Shanghai Municipal Orchestra. An elderly Russian music master supporting himself by teaching in Qingdao and Beiping, who takes Helen as a pupil, belongs squarely to that world. The name 史托亦夫斯基 is romanized here as Stoyevsky; no external attestation. Corroborated as a milieu.

ch42.anchor: To find, in this world of mine
ch42.note: From here to the end of the chapter the narrator sets down extracts he has copied from Bai Ping’s silver diary (introduced at the close of Chapter 41). The passages headed ‘My note:’ are his own, interpolated to decode her private shorthand—the coded words ‘business,’ ‘clientele,’ the ‘banquet’ and the rest—while the dashes and rows of dots mark where he has broken off, or passed a passage over. The diary is thus doubly voiced: hers, and his reading of hers.

The remembered speaker here is Mei Yingzi, taking Bai Ping’s hand to admire the ring Xu had given her. The diary slips without warning into the recorded words of others—one of the ‘queer expressions and simple symbols’ the narrator has said he must guess at.

ch43.note: State Express 555 (from its trademark number, ‘555’) was a British American Tobacco brand and one of the most popular imported cigarettes in China in this period; Lucky Strike was the well-known American brand. The single Lucky Strike slipped in among Bai Ping’s 555s serves as the marked lot, so that whoever presses it out of the case draws the task.

The ‘interior’ (后方, lit. ‘the rear’) is unoccupied Free China—the vast hinterland behind the war fronts, governed from the wartime capital at Chongqing. To ‘go to the interior’ meant leaving occupied Shanghai to join the resistance, as against merely moving to Japanese-held Beiping.

ch44.note: Korea had been a colony of Japan since the annexation of 1910, and many Koreans worked in Japanese-run teahouses and cabarets across occupied China; this is why Miko, whom the narrator had taken for a Japanese, is in fact Korean.

ch45.anchor: a bottle that had held quinine
ch45.note: Quinine (金鸡纳霜, from the cinchona bark) was the ordinary anti-malarial of the day; the everyday medicine bottle is a blind for the three poison pills. In their private code the two of them will speak of these pills, too, as the narrator’s ‘aspirin.’

ch46.anchor: the gambling den on Columbia Road
ch46.note: Mei Yingzi asks, in a private code, whether her two collaborators have both come—Bai Ping (“the Xujiahui church”) and Miko (“the gambling den on Columbia Road”); the narrator understands her at once. Columbia Road (歌伦比亚路, Columbia Avenue) was a real road in the far west of Shanghai, laid out by the Municipal Council in 1925 and renamed Panyu Road (番禺路) only in 1943, so its old name fits the novel’s wartime setting.

ch47.note: The code arises from the previous chapter: the narrator squirted ink from his fountain pen onto the intruding woman’s trailing skirt, and the dried spray—seven or eight dots in a line—looks like a small snake, which Bai Ping and Mei Yingzi take up as their name for the marked woman. The source varies the epithet: here 蓝色响尾蛇 (‘blue rattlesnake’), and later 蓝尾蛇 (‘blue-tailed snake’) and 蓝色的小蛇 (‘little blue snake’); the variation is kept.

Manchukuo (满洲国) was the puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast (Manchuria) in 1932, nominally ruled by Puyi, the last Qing emperor, and dissolved in 1945. The exchange is pointed: the woman speaks of Manchukuo as a land apart from China, and the narrator retorts that it never once occurred to him it was anything but Chinese soil.

ch48.note: The demure ‘Miyama Yoshiko’ of Honsa’s dinner is revealed as the intruder at the safe, now speaking fluent Mandarin and giving her name as Asamura Toshimiko. Both names are Japanese and are read tentatively here, the source offering no romanization; the surname 宫间 (Miyama) is the same as that of 宫间登水 (Miyama Toshimi), the admirer who sent Bai Ping flowers in hospital, and the element 登水 recurs in 登水子 (Toshimiko).

ch49.note: Kawashima Yoshiko (川岛芳子, 1907–1948) was a real historical figure: born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, a Manchu princess of the fallen Qing imperial house, she was raised in Japan by the adventurer Kawashima Naniwa and became a spy for the Japanese Kwantung Army and the puppet state of Manchukuo, notorious for dressing as a man and for commanding troops of her own. She was executed for treason by the Chinese Nationalist government in 1948. The intercepted report makes Miyama Yoshiko her long-time follower; corroborated as to Kawashima herself.

Lang Diyi (郎第仪) and Akiu Saburo (秋雨三郎) are the two cover-names the report assigns Miyama Yoshiko — the first carried among Chinese, the second the man's name under which she is said to range through Japanese military and political circles. The source gives no romanization for either, so both readings here are provisional; the mannish alias deliberately echoes the real Kawashima Yoshiko, famed for the same disguise.

Edinburgh Road (忆定盘路, today Jiangsu Road) ran north–south through the western part of the International Settlement; the Chinese name 忆定盘 is simply a transliteration of ‘Edinburgh.’ The Yuyuan Road address Miyama gives the narrator here, at the Edinburgh Road corner, lies in a quite different quarter from the Youheng Road house in Hongkou where the intelligence of the previous chapter placed her real residence.

ch51.note: Tche San, Teh-San, Tche-San: the boat family's speech renders the girl's name in the sounds of their own dialect, which the narrator hears and maps onto the Mandarin name Cishan (慈珊). The coincidence that so unsettles him is that Cishan was also the name he had once invented for a fictitious country girl in the decoy letters of an earlier chapter.

The boat people (船户) were the poor who lived aboard the sampans and cargo junks moored gunwale to gunwale along Suzhou Creek, washing, cooking, and sleeping on the water — a distinct and destitute river community of wartime Shanghai, among whom the narrator and Mei Yingzi now take refuge.

Sealing off a district (封锁) was a standard Japanese response to any ‘incident’ in occupied Shanghai: barbed wire and rope barriers flung across the streets of a quarter, with soldiers questioning everyone who tried to pass, so as to trap a fugitive inside. It is what has just closed around the narrator and Mei Yingzi after the shooting.

ch52.anchor: on no account tell anyone you have guests here
ch52.note: The source is garbled at this point: it reads, literally, ‘first, you must by all means tell people you have guests here’ (第一万要告诉人你有客人在这里), which reverses Mei Yingzi's plain intent, since she is arranging to stay hidden. A negative has evidently dropped out (第一，千万[不]要…), and the sense is restored here rather than reproduced as it stands.

‘White powder’ (白面, literally ‘white flour’) was the common street name for heroin in Republican-era Shanghai. A jiao (角) was a tenth of a yuan; the addicts' fixed daily need of eight jiao — four in the morning, four in the afternoon — measures out lives narrowed to a single craving, in one of the bleakest passages of the book.

Mei Lanfang (梅兰芳, 1894–1961) was the most celebrated Peking-opera performer of his age, renowned above all for his female roles (旦). ‘The Heavenly Maiden Scatters Flowers’ (天女散花), which he devised and first staged in 1917, drew on the Vimalakīrti Sutra and on the Dunhuang cave paintings and was famous for its ribbon dance; a colored stage photograph of him in the part is what backs the boat girl's little mirror.

The paired character is 寿 (shou), ‘long life’ — one of the commonest auspicious emblems in Chinese ornament, worn as a charm for longevity and good fortune. The narrator reads Mei Yingzi's borrowed 寿 earrings as a good omen, in pointed contrast to Bai Ping's ‘lucky earrings,’ which had filled him with dread just before she was shot.

ch53.note: The boat family are named by the Chinese reckoning of kin by seniority. Bingfu addresses Cishan’s mother as 二婶 (er shen), ‘Second Auntie,’ the wife of the second brother; the boatman who saves them is 三叔 (san shu), ‘Third Uncle,’ the father’s third younger brother; and Bingfu’s own father is 大伯 (da bo), the eldest uncle. The numbers rank the brothers by age, not by count, and are kept here as relational titles.

The mother’s phrase is 野鸡生意 (yeji shengyi, literally ‘wild-pheasant business’), Shanghai slang for unlicensed, off-the-books work — here the Third Uncle’s illicit night ferrying of goods, the very trade that lets him smuggle the pair ashore.
小黑子 (Xiao Heizi), the boy who crews Cishan’s Third Uncle’s boat; the nickname means ‘Little Blackie,’ a common affectionate name for a dark-skinned child. Romanized here in pinyin.

ch54.note: The source names the road by its Shanghai nickname 法大马路 (Fada malu, ‘the French great road’), the colloquial name for the Rue du Consulat (公馆马路) in the French Concession, its chief east–west thoroughfare, lined with small hotels and lodging-houses; today East Jinling Road. Corroborated.

The white cloth reads 陶宅寄存, ‘held in deposit for the Tao residence.’ Bai Ping (a stage name) is thus disclosed to have been a 陶 (Tao) — the surname of the household the cases were entered under; the source lets the label carry the revelation without spelling it out.

ch55.note: Xu Xu wrote The Whistling Wind in 1943, in the war’s darkest stretch; the narrator’s dream of an enemy who has ‘surrendered unconditionally’ and a war already passed into the history textbooks anticipates by two years the event itself — Japan’s unconditional surrender of August 1945. In the dream it is a longing, not yet history. Corroborated as to the later event.
三妹 (san mei, ‘Third Sister’) is the name Mei Yingzi gives on the telephone — a cover-name for the wire, as the narrator himself hides under ‘Chen Ji.’

ch56.anchor: did Bai Ping foreknow her own death
ch56.note: Before setting out, Bai Ping had disposed of her keepsakes as one who does not expect to return — the cat Jimi to Mrs. Manfield, the diamond ring (the one she and the narrator had exchanged, Chapter 6) to Helen, the silver diary to Mei Yingzi, and to the narrator the portrait he had drawn of her asleep. The narrator reads it against the will she had made him write before the theft at Umetake’s (Chapter 45): a second sign that she went to Youheng Road knowing she might not come back.

ch56.anchor: the head of the military's press bureau
ch56.note: 军部报导部 (the Hōdōbu), the press-and-information department of the Japanese military, which controlled and censored the news in occupied China; that the murdered woman is niece to its chief marks how high in the enemy’s apparatus she stood. Corroborated as an institution.

ch57.note: The note and Miko’s sung reply exchange two song titles as a private token of recognition: the narrator writes ‘the Sunset over the Huangpu’ (黄浦江头的落日, the Huangpu being Shanghai’s river), and Miko answers by announcing a Chinese song, ‘Autumn Green amid the Cries of the Flower-Sellers’ (卖花声里的秋绿). Whether these name real songs or are invented for the scene the source does not say.

ch58.note: A huanxiang zheng (还乡证, ‘returning-home permit’), the pass a resident of Japanese-occupied Shanghai needed in order to travel out of the city into the unoccupied interior. Securing one was the practical first step in slipping away to Free China, and the narrator’s quiet acquisition of it marks his decision as irreversible.

The word rendered ‘journey’ is zhengtu (征途), the road of a campaign or a mission rather than a mere trip. Ending the novel on it returns the reader to the book’s title, The Whistling Wind (风萧萧), which echoes the parting song of the assassin Jing Ke—‘the wind whistles, cold runs the Yi’—a man setting out on a mission from which he will not return. The wind and the streaming cloud of the last lines sound that note of high, doomed departure one final time.

ch59.note: This appendix gathers five appreciations of Xu Xu published in Hong Kong’s Apple Daily (苹果日报) in October and November 2013, more than thirty years after his death; they are not by Xu Xu, and are given here in the order the source prints them. Joseph S. M. Lau (Liu Shaoming, 刘绍铭) was a scholar of modern Chinese literature and one of the co-translators of C. T. Hsia’s history into Chinese.

ch59.anchor: A History of Modern Chinese Fiction
ch59.note: C. T. Hsia (Xia Zhiqing, 夏志清, 1921–2013) published A History of Modern Chinese Fiction with Yale University Press in 1961. The study is generally credited with founding the modern Western canon of the field and with raising Eileen Chang, Qian Zhongshu, and Shen Congwen to prominence; its silence on Xu Xu—by the mid-1940s a far more popular writer—is the wound the first two essays here keep pressing.

ch59.anchor: The country folk fondly called him The Knight of Sorrowful Countenance
ch59.note: ‘The Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance’ (Spanish el Caballero de la Triste Figura) is the title Don Quixote gives himself in Part I of Cervantes’s novel. Liu Shaoming borrows it for Xu Xu’s gaunt, melancholy face; the English phrase stands in the source itself as the title of this first essay.

Lin Yutang (林语堂, 1895–1976), who coined the Chinese loanword youmo (幽默) for ‘humour,’ edited a run of light-essay magazines—The Analects Fortnightly (论语, 1932), This Human World (人间世, 1934), and Cosmic Wind—that made the leisurely familiar essay a vogue and drew Lu Xun’s repeated attack. Xu Xu served as his editorial assistant.

Corroborated. After the March 18, 1926 massacre in Beijing, in which government troops fired on student demonstrators, the Duan Qirui (段祺瑞) government issued warrants for the arrest of intellectuals. Lu Xun’s friend Xu Shoushang recalled a list of ‘fifty—in fact only forty-eight names,’ Lu Xun among them; this essay places Lin Yutang on the same roll. Lu Xun called it ‘the darkest day since the founding of the Republic.’

Lu Xun (鲁迅, pen name of Zhou Shuren, 周树人, 1881–1936), author of The True Story of Ah Q, is the towering figure of modern Chinese letters; the third essay reconstructs his guarded, elder-to-junior dealings with the young Xu Xu. In the mistranslation quoted just here, ‘Lu Hsun’ is the older Wade-Giles spelling of the same name.

The bagu wen (八股文, ‘eight-legged essay’) was the rigidly formulaic composition demanded in the imperial civil-service examinations; by extension it means stale, formula-bound prose. Xu Xu’s point is that the leisured essays of Lin Yutang’s magazines cut through the stiff, sloganizing writing of the day.

Contradicted. John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946) came from an English Congregationalist family and called himself an agnostic; he was not Jewish. He had also died in 1946, so he was not personally the framer of Britain’s economic policy in the 1950s, though the postwar settlement of welfare and full employment was built on Keynesian ideas. The error is the essayist’s, kept and corrected here rather than silently amended.
